title: Hypertension: Diagnose Correctly, Then Treat Absolute Risk
bottomLine: Use standardized validated blood-pressure measurement and confirm persistent hypertension with repeated and preferably out-of-office measurements when appropriate. Under Hypertension Canada 2025, hypertension is defined at 130/80 mmHg or higher with optimal measurement, while medication initiation and treatment intensity still depend on blood-pressure level, cardiovascular risk, comorbidity and tolerability rather than the diagnostic threshold alone.
recognize: White-coat and masked hypertension are common enough that home or ambulatory measurements can materially change diagnosis.
Secondary hypertension becomes more likely with abrupt onset, resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, unusual age of onset or a suggestive clinical syndrome.
differentiate: A diagnostic threshold is not automatically the medication-start threshold for every low-risk patient.
Hypertensive emergency requires acute target-organ injury; severe asymptomatic hypertension is not the same syndrome.
assessment: Confirm cuff size and technique, repeat measurements, review home readings, smoking, diabetes, CKD, lipids, sleep apnea, medications and substances that raise BP, pregnancy potential and orthostatic symptoms.
workup: Use basic renal, electrolyte, glycemic and lipid assessment plus ECG and cause-directed testing; investigate secondary hypertension when probability is meaningful rather than ordering a universal endocrine panel.
management: Use lifestyle treatment for all appropriate patients and initiate pharmacotherapy according to current Hypertension Canada blood-pressure and cardiovascular-risk thresholds; for many patients requiring drug treatment, a low-dose two-drug combination from recommended first-line classes is preferred.
Aim for the current recommended systolic treatment target when tolerated while individualizing for frailty, orthostasis and competing risk.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy and should not be combined routinely; thiazide-like diuretics can alter sodium and potassium, and calcium-channel blockers can cause edema.
counselling: Teach home BP technique and explain the difference between diagnosis, treatment threshold and treatment target.
followUp: Reassess BP, orthostasis, electrolytes and renal function after meaningful treatment changes and use home or ambulatory data when needed to confirm control.
examTrap: Starting or escalating medication from one hurried office reading without confirming technique, persistence or cardiovascular risk context.
oneLinePearl: Hypertension is a measured pattern plus risk—not one isolated cuff value.

title: Asthma: Confirm Variable Airflow Disease and Use ICS-Containing Control
bottomLine: Asthma is variable respiratory symptoms plus variable expiratory airflow limitation. Whenever feasible, confirm the diagnosis objectively and use an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing treatment strategy rather than chronic SABA-only management; acute severity is determined by work of breathing, speech, oxygenation, airflow and response to treatment.
recognize: Episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnea that vary over time or with triggers support asthma.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; variability may require repeat spirometry, peak-flow monitoring or bronchoprovocation.
differentiate: COPD causes more persistent airflow obstruction in the appropriate exposure context; inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, reflux and anxiety can mimic asthma symptoms.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nighttime waking, reliever use, exacerbations, oral steroid bursts, ED visits, triggers, smoking or vaping, occupational exposure, adherence and inhaler technique.
workup: Use quality spirometry with bronchodilator response when feasible and alternative objective testing when spirometry is nondiagnostic but probability remains high.
management: Use an ICS-containing controller or anti-inflammatory reliever strategy appropriate to age and severity under current Canadian guidance; step treatment up only after checking diagnosis, adherence, technique, exposures and comorbidity.
Treat significant exacerbations promptly with inhaled bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroid when indicated, oxygen and escalation for poor response or severe physiology.
medicationSafety: Repeated SABA use without anti-inflammatory treatment is a risk signal, not adequate disease control; repeated systemic corticosteroid bursts create cumulative toxicity.
redFlags: Silent chest or minimal air movement
counselling: Teach inhaler and spacer technique, trigger reduction, written action plan and when worsening requires urgent care.
followUp: Reassess control and technique after exacerbation and step down only after sustained control when appropriate.
examTrap: Refilling frequent SABA indefinitely without adding or optimizing inhaled anti-inflammatory therapy or checking why control is poor.
oneLinePearl: Asthma is an inflammatory airway disease; bronchodilation alone does not control the disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Asthma Guideline and focused updates

title: Type 2 Diabetes: Glycemia Plus Cardiorenal Risk
bottomLine: Type 2 diabetes treatment is no longer chosen from A1C alone. Set an individualized glycemic goal, then deliberately address established or high-risk atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure and CKD because SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists can provide organ protection in selected patients beyond glucose lowering.
recognize: A1C, fasting glucose and glucose-challenge testing have defined diagnostic roles, but A1C can be misleading when red-cell turnover or hemoglobin variants materially alter it.
Diabetes complications include kidney, retinal, neurologic and cardiovascular disease and should be screened systematically.
differentiate: Type 1 diabetes, LADA, steroid-induced diabetes, pancreatogenic diabetes and monogenic diabetes should be reconsidered when the phenotype or treatment response is atypical.
assessment: Assess glycemic symptoms and data, hypoglycemia, weight and nutrition, ASCVD, HF, eGFR and albuminuria, retinopathy, neuropathy/feet, medications, cost/access, pregnancy and treatment goals.
workup: Confirm diagnosis appropriately and monitor A1C or alternative glycemic data, kidney function and urine albumin, lipids, retinal status and foot risk at guideline-supported intervals.
management: Use lifestyle and pharmacotherapy individualized to glycemia, organ protection, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, kidney function, cost and preference; prioritize agents with proven cardiorenal benefit when the corresponding comorbidity is present.
Use insulin promptly when marked symptomatic hyperglycemia, catabolism, ketosis or another insulin-requiring state makes delay unsafe.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause genital infection and euglycemic DKA and require perioperative or acute-illness hold planning; GLP-1 receptor agonists commonly cause GI effects; sulfonylureas and insulin increase hypoglycemia risk.
redFlags: Progressive CKD or diabetic foot infection
counselling: Use shared goals and avoid framing medication escalation as personal failure.
followUp: Review glycemic response, organ-protective therapy, tolerability and access after treatment changes and at regular chronic-care intervals.
examTrap: Choosing the next glucose-lowering drug only from the A1C while ignoring heart failure, CKD or established ASCVD.
oneLinePearl: In type 2 diabetes, treat glucose and protect the heart and kidneys at the same time.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada 2024 Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes

title: Sepsis: Recognize Organ Dysfunction, Treat Shock Immediately, Reassess Continuously
system: Acute Care / Infectious Disease / Critical Care
bottomLine: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection. In septic shock or a very high-likelihood sepsis presentation, obtain cultures when they do not create dangerous delay, start appropriate antimicrobials promptly, restore perfusion and use norepinephrine first-line when vasopressor support is required; fluid should be reassessed dynamically rather than continued by rote.
recognize: Hypotension, altered mental status, tachypnea, hypoxemia, oliguria, lactate elevation, coagulopathy or acute organ injury can indicate sepsis even without fever.
Older or immunocompromised patients can present with subtle temperature or white-cell changes.
differentiate: Cardiogenic, hemorrhagic, obstructive and anaphylactic shock can mimic distributive sepsis physiology and may coexist with infection.
qSOFA can flag risk but should not be used as the sole sepsis screening or diagnostic rule.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, perfusion, mental status, urine output, likely source, immune status, indwelling devices, prior resistant organisms and recent antimicrobials.
workup: Obtain blood cultures and source-specific microbiology when feasible before antibiotics, plus lactate and organ-function testing; image the suspected source when it can change source control without delaying resuscitation.
management: Give prompt empiric antimicrobials in shock or high-likelihood sepsis and tailor them to source, severity and resistance risk, then de-escalate when data permit.

Give initial balanced crystalloid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion while repeatedly reassessing fluid responsiveness and overload; start norepinephrine when hypotension persists and pursue early source control.
medicationSafety: Avoid reflexively continuing broad-spectrum therapy after cultures and clinical evolution support narrowing; excessive fluid can worsen pulmonary edema and abdominal or tissue edema.
counselling: After recovery, explain medication changes, unresolved infection-source issues and post-sepsis functional or cognitive symptoms.
followUp: Review culture results, antimicrobial duration, organ recovery and post-discharge rehabilitation needs.
examTrap: Treating sepsis as a fixed one-size-fits-all litre-and-timer bundle without reassessing whether the patient is fluid responsive, overloaded or in another shock state.
oneLinePearl: Sepsis resuscitation is urgent and iterative: treat, measure response, and treat again.
sourceBasis: Canadian critical-care and antimicrobial-stewardship practice principles

title: Acute Ischemic Stroke and TIA: Time-Critical Imaging and Secondary Prevention
bottomLine: New focal neurologic deficit is stroke until proven otherwise and requires immediate stroke-capable assessment, glucose check and brain/vascular imaging. Reperfusion eligibility is time- and imaging-dependent, while high-risk TIA also requires urgent same-day evaluation and rapid secondary prevention rather than routine delayed referral.
recognize: Face, arm or leg weakness, aphasia, visual-field loss, neglect, ataxia and sudden severe posterior-circulation symptoms can represent stroke.
Posterior circulation stroke may present with diplopia, dysarthria, severe gait/truncal ataxia or vertigo without classic FAST weakness.
differentiate: Hypoglycemia, seizure with Todd paralysis, migraine aura and functional neurologic disorder can mimic stroke but should not create delay when stroke remains plausible.
assessment: Establish exact last-known-well or symptom-discovery time, glucose, BP, anticoagulants, recent surgery/bleeding, baseline function and a focused neurologic severity assessment.
workup: Obtain emergent noncontrast brain imaging plus vascular imaging according to the stroke pathway; selected patients may require advanced perfusion imaging for extended-window endovascular treatment decisions.
management: Activate reperfusion pathways immediately for eligible ischemic stroke and treat BP according to reperfusion and stroke subtype requirements; do not give antiplatelet therapy until hemorrhage is excluded.
For TIA or minor stroke, initiate urgent mechanism-directed secondary prevention and appropriate antiplatelet or anticoagulation strategy after imaging and risk assessment.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation is not an acute substitute for thrombolysis in ischemic stroke; antithrombotic timing after thrombolysis or hemorrhage follows stroke-specific protocols.
counselling: Teach patients that transient deficits are still an emergency because early recurrent stroke risk can be high.
followUp: Close the loop on vascular imaging, AF monitoring, lipids/BP, antithrombotic therapy and rehabilitation using current Canadian Stroke Best Practices.
examTrap: Scheduling a routine clinic appointment weeks later for a patient whose unilateral weakness and aphasia fully resolved after 20 minutes today.
oneLinePearl: A TIA is a stroke warning with an urgent clock, not a reassuring resolved symptom.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices Acute Stroke Management 2025
Canadian Stroke Best Practices Secondary Prevention

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Stability, Stroke Prevention, Rate or Rhythm Strategy
bottomLine: Atrial fibrillation management starts with hemodynamic stability, then stroke-prevention eligibility, symptom control and treatment of triggers or comorbidity. Anticoagulation decisions are based on validated Canadian thromboembolic-risk guidance—not on whether the AF is paroxysmal or currently back in sinus rhythm.
recognize: AF produces an irregular atrial rhythm without consistent organized P waves and can be symptomatic or discovered incidentally.
Triggers and contributors include infection, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, ischemia, heart failure and sleep apnea.
differentiate: Atrial flutter may have organized flutter waves; frequent ectopy can create an irregular pulse without AF; pre-excited AF is dangerous and managed differently.
assessment: Assess stability, symptom onset and burden, stroke and bleeding risk, renal function, structural heart disease, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, alcohol and reversible triggers.
workup: Confirm with ECG or rhythm recording and obtain selected CBC, electrolytes, renal and thyroid tests plus echocardiography when appropriate.
management: Perform urgent synchronized cardioversion for hemodynamic instability attributable to AF.

For stable AF, choose rate and/or rhythm control according to symptoms, duration, comorbidity and patient preference, and prescribe anticoagulation according to current Canadian stroke-prevention criteria; DOACs are preferred for many eligible patients but are not appropriate for mechanical valves and selected valvular conditions.
medicationSafety: Renal function and interactions affect DOAC dosing; AV-nodal blockers can worsen bradycardia or decompensated heart failure; AV-nodal blockade alone can be dangerous in pre-excited AF.
counselling: Explain that stroke risk can persist even when episodes are intermittent and that anticoagulation is preventive, not a rhythm-control drug.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, rhythm strategy, anticoagulation adherence/dose, renal function and modifiable AF risk factors.
examTrap: Stopping anticoagulation solely because a paroxysmal-AF patient is in sinus rhythm at today's visit.
oneLinePearl: Sinus rhythm today does not erase AF-related stroke risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society atrial fibrillation guidance

title: HFrEF: Build Foundational Therapy, Treat Congestion, Reassess the Patient
bottomLine: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is treated with early foundational disease-modifying therapy using an ARNI or appropriate RAAS inhibitor, an evidence-based beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor when tolerated, while loop diuretics treat congestion rather than mortality risk. Titrate the whole regimen while following BP, renal function, potassium and symptoms.
recognize: Dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, elevated JVP and congestion support HF but can be absent between exacerbations.
A falling ejection fraction requires evaluation for ischemic, valvular, arrhythmic, toxic or inflammatory causes.
differentiate: HFpEF has preserved EF and a different evidence base; COPD, obesity and renal disease can mimic congestion or dyspnea.
assessment: Assess volume status, NYHA symptoms, BP, renal function, potassium, heart rate/rhythm, adherence, NSAIDs, ischemia and valvular disease.
workup: Use ECG, natriuretic peptide when diagnosis is uncertain, echocardiography and cause-directed ischemic or other testing.
management: Start and sequence the foundational HFrEF drug classes early at tolerated doses rather than waiting to maximize one class before introducing the others; use loop diuretics to achieve euvolemia.
Evaluate device, iron deficiency, cardiac rehabilitation and specialty referral based on EF, rhythm and persistent symptoms.
medicationSafety: Monitor potassium and renal function with RAAS inhibition and MRAs; avoid routine NSAIDs; beta blockers are initiated or titrated cautiously during unstable decompensation.
counselling: Teach daily symptom and weight monitoring, sodium/fluid advice individualized to disease severity, medication purpose and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: Reassess BP, renal function, potassium and congestion soon after initiation or titration and repeat EF when it will change device or treatment decisions.
examTrap: Treating chronic HFrEF primarily with furosemide while omitting the disease-modifying foundational drug classes.
oneLinePearl: Diuretics make HFrEF patients feel drier; foundational therapy helps them live longer.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Heart Failure Guidelines and focused updates

title: Febrile Infant 90 Days or Younger: Age, Appearance, Inflammatory Markers, and Reliable Follow-Up
bottomLine: A rectal temperature of 38.0°C or higher in a well-appearing infant 90 days or younger requires age-stratified assessment for invasive bacterial infection using the current Canadian Paediatric Society pathway. The youngest infants have the lowest threshold for blood, urine, CSF evaluation, empiric antibiotics and admission; selected older low-risk infants can be managed less invasively only when validated criteria and reliable follow-up are satisfied.
recognize: Young infants can have invasive bacterial infection without focal findings or toxic appearance.
Urinary tract infection is common, but bacteremia and bacterial meningitis are the cannot-miss outcomes driving the age-based pathway.
differentiate: A documented viral infection can reduce—but does not eliminate—bacterial infection risk and should not automatically cancel age-appropriate urine or invasive-bacterial-infection assessment.
assessment: Confirm reliable rectal temperature, exact age in days, gestational history, appearance, feeding, perfusion, respiratory status, focal symptoms, perinatal infection risk and ability for rapid reassessment.
workup: Follow the current CPS 2026 age-group pathway for urinalysis/culture, blood culture, inflammatory markers and lumbar puncture decisions; use a properly collected urine specimen rather than bag culture to diagnose UTI.
management: Treat any ill-appearing infant as high risk with immediate stabilization, cultures and empiric antimicrobials.
For well-appearing infants, use the CPS age-stratified risk algorithm to determine lumbar puncture, antibiotics, observation, admission or carefully structured outpatient follow-up.
medicationSafety: Empiric antibiotic and antiviral choices are age-, syndrome- and local-resistance-specific; suspected neonatal HSV requires urgent acyclovir coverage and appropriate testing.
counselling: Give explicit return precautions and ensure caregivers understand that deterioration can be rapid even after a reassuring first examination.
followUp: For any outpatient pathway, ensure timely reassessment and active review of blood and urine cultures rather than passive 'call if worse' follow-up.
examTrap: Sending a 3-week-old well-appearing febrile infant home because a respiratory viral test is positive.
oneLinePearl: In the febrile young infant, exact age in days changes the whole pathway.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society: Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Young Infants Aged 90 Days or Younger, updated 2026
